analysis.one_liner: Curbs speculative trading in energy and farm commodities with position limits, tougher reporting, and offshore loophole closures.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 283-133, but the Senate never voted: the bill died in the Senate Agriculture Committee when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After oil and gasoline prices spiked in 2008, this bill directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to set limits on how large a speculative bet any one trader could hold in energy and agricultural futures, forced big index funds and swap dealers to report their positions, and required foreign exchanges offering US traders access to energy contracts to follow rules comparable to US exchanges. It also added at least 100 CFTC staff for transparency and enforcement. The House passed it by a wide bipartisan margin, but it never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers facing gasoline, heating oil, and food prices, who the bill's premise says were paying a premium driven by excessive speculation in commodity markets. Farmers and airlines and other businesses that physically buy or sell commodities would also benefit from tighter limits on speculators and from public data showing how much of the market is speculative versus hedging.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of gasoline, energy, and food

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CFTC to set position limits on speculative holdings in agricultural and energy commodity markets, with limits on spot-month, single-month, and all-months aggregate positions [S3][S4].

Closes a key loophole by barring foreign exchanges from giving US-located traders direct access to energy and agricultural contracts unless they publish comparable data and adopt comparable position limits, and it brings previously exempted foreign boards under the rule after 180 days [S3][S4].

Subjects index traders, swap dealers, and large over-the-counter traders to routine detailed reporting and recordkeeping, and directs the CFTC to publicly disaggregate index-fund positions from bona fide hedgers so the public can see how speculative the market is [S3][S4].
Directs the CFTC to hire at least 100 new full-time employees to increase market transparency and improve enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large speculators, hedge funds, index traders, and swap dealers who had been trading energy and agricultural derivatives with little oversight, plus foreign exchanges that profit from offering US traders a route around US rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large commodity speculators and swap dealers

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates position limits for speculators within 60 days of enactment and directs the CFTC to bring over-the-counter and offshore trades under comparable rules, an aggressive intervention in markets that had operated largely outside those limits [S3][S4].

It imposes new reporting and recordkeeping duties on swap dealers, index traders, and large over-the-counter traders, including 5-year record retention open to CFTC and Justice Department inspection, a real compliance cost for financial firms [S4].

The bill's premise — that speculation drove the 2008 price spike — was contested: many economists argued prices were set by supply and demand, and position limits could reduce market liquidity that hedgers rely on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If speculation was inflating energy and food prices, the bill attacked the problem directly and cheaply for consumers, at real cost to speculators and derivatives dealers. The honest caveat is that the causal case was disputed — the CFTC's own interim analysis that summer found limited evidence speculation was the main driver of oil prices — so the bill could have imposed compliance costs and reduced liquidity without delivering much price relief. Even so, the transparency provisions alone (publishing what share of the market is speculative, closing unmonitored offshore routes) were low-risk measures, and Congress later adopted similar swap-reporting and position-limit authorities in the 2010 Dodd-Frank law.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 283-133, but the Senate Agriculture Committee received it in October 2008 and never acted, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 24, 2008, and referred to the House Agriculture Committee [S1][S6].

A first attempt to pass it on July 30 under a suspension of the rules — a fast track requiring a two-thirds majority — failed 276-151, with Democrats in favor 215-16 and Republicans opposed 61-135 [S6][S7].
The House brought it back on September 18 under a rule barring amendments; a Republican motion to recommit with instructions failed 196-221 along party lines [S6][S8].
The bill passed the House on September 18, 2008, 283-133: 214 of 234 voting Democrats in favor, 69 of 199 Republicans in favor [S6][S9].

The Senate received the bill on September 22 and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on October 2, 2008, where it received no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large commodity speculators, swap dealers, and offshore exchanges kept trading energy and agricultural derivatives without position limits or the new reporting requirements. The bill's later ideas partly resurfaced in the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act, but for the remainder of the 110th Congress no new limits or transparency rules took effect.

for.name: Collin Peterson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, moved to pass it as amended, and steered it through a closed rule to House passage 283-133.

for.name: 214 of 236 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, providing nearly all of the vote total.

against.name: 119 of 199 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, and 135 of them had blocked the earlier two-thirds-vote attempt in July.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 2, 2008, and never reported it out; the Senate never voted on it.

against.name: Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's approach, arguing mandatory position limits and offshore restrictions could backfire on energy markets and prices.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was 283-133, but the parties diverged sharply: 214 of 234 voting Democrats voted yes versus 69 of 199 Republicans, and an earlier July attempt failed 276-151 with 135 of 199 Republicans voting no; the Senate never voted.

industries.industry: Commodity speculators, hedge funds, and swap dealers
industries.note: The bill subjects their large energy and agricultural positions to mandatory limits, detailed reporting, and 5-year recordkeeping, ending the largely unmonitored over-the-counter and offshore routes they used. Their profits from unregulated speculation came at the cost of the price volatility consumers paid at the pump, per the bill's own findings.

industries.industry: Foreign futures exchanges (offshore boards of trade)
industries.note: Exchanges such as London-based venues offering US traders direct access to energy contracts would have to publish comparable data and adopt comparable position limits or lose that access. The bill's premise was that they had served as an escape hatch from US limits.

industries.industry: US commodity exchanges and index funds
industries.note: Registered exchanges face new core-principle duties to adopt speculator position limits, and index traders face new reporting, but bona fide hedgers keep their exemptions and the bill preserves the exchange-based market structure. The added transparency could stabilize markets these firms depend on.
